speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Prime Minister, of which 1 gave his office notice. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry. Can he now inform the house of the cause of the pollution of the waters of Placentia and St. Marys Bays. speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of Fisheries and Forestry):
subtopic: PLACENTIA BAY, NFLD.-TRACING OF POLLUTION TO SOURCE AT CHEMICAL PLANT

Mr. Speaker, last night I received an oral report from our scientists who are at work in the Placentia Bay area. They inform me that they are now certain that the cause of the pollution is phosphorus, discharged by the chemical plant of the area. The plant has since been shut down. subtopic: A.B.M. SYSTEM-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY-REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S.
A.B.M. SYSTEM-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY-REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Since construction of the A.B.M. safeguard system has been begun in the United States and since the Prime Minister in an earlier statement to this house said that Canada's attitude to the system and participation in it

would be based on whether it contributed to war or peace, or to the escalation of the arms race, will the Prime Minister in the near future make a statement to this house on the government's attitude toward this system?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minisier):
subtopic: A.B.M. SYSTEM-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY-REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hope I did not leave the impression that we wanted to participate actively in this system. I indicated that the position we would have to take in judging this system would be based on whether it increases the possibility of nuclear arms escalation or whether it decreases it. We have not reached any conclusion on this yet.

subtopic: A.B.M. SYSTEM-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY-REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S.
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Will the Prime Minister let the house know what the government's attitude is to this system before the house adjourns for the summer?

subtopic: A.B.M. SYSTEM-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY-REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the attitude of the government, I think, would not be very different from the attitude of the opposition. We are not enthusiastic about the system, but this is a defence system being built in another country. Whether it will prevent a nuclear holocaust is a consideration that is in all our minds. But we cannot be pressed into making any rapid decisions about the defence systems of other nations, whether they be the Soviet Union, Japan, China or other countries. We are busy now considering our own defence systems and our own policies for defence.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: A.B.M. SYSTEM-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY-REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S.
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Am I to assume from the Prime Minister's statement that there has been some modification in the government's attitude as expressed by the Prime Minister during the debate in this house? Was not the government's attitude that it felt it necessary to assess the significance of the measures proposed by the President of the United States and felt obliged to condemn the system if it concluded that the proposed measures taken by the United States are not in the interests of the world peace? Has that attitude changed? Has my right hon. friend decided that this question should be left entirely to the decision of the United States?

subtopic: A.B.M. SYSTEM-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY-REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S.
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. The position is still the same. We realize it is important to make this assessment. What I am saying is that it is not likely that any moral judgment we might enunciate will have a great deal of effect on the United States position. The moral judgment that we can make
May 23, 1969



could equally well be made by the Leader of the Opposition or by the leader of the New Democratic party. This will be, as I say, a moral decision taken by friendly nations. But debate is going on in the United States, and if their policy is to remain or is to be changed, that decision will come about as a consequence of what is happening in the United States debate and not as a consequence of statements made in this house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: A.B.M. SYSTEM-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY-REPRESENTATIONS TO U.S.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE- APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, May 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mac-Eachen (for Mr. Trudeau) that Bill C-120, respecting the status of the official languages of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Special Committee on the Official Languages Bill.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE- APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this point in our consideration of Bill C-120 concerning the official languages of Canada we are deciding whether or not to send the bill to a committee for consideration. We are not deciding the details of the legislation but rather the simple question of whether or not a bill of this type is worthy of further study.
This bill must be regarded as civil rights legislation. In order to have the right perspective we must look at what is happening in other parts of the world such as the United States, Britain and Africa. We should not assume that the demand for enlargement of the rights of minorities will not reach the same fever pitch in Canada that it has in other countries. The facts and the background are different but the human feelings are the same. I believe this bill is a mild forerunner of some of the jarring and traumatic civil rights legislation we may be called upon to consider in this country before very long. If we fail to face up to our responsibilities at this point we will be failing all those who follow us.
The legislation is not in the form in which I should like to see it. Many of the reasons have been expounded by others. Unfortunately the Liberal government has the responsibility for introducing legislation and it has drafted the bill in this way. We must make efforts to put it in better shape, but that does not mean that we can be against it. This does not affect my belief that recognition must be given to the grievances, which have existed for many years, of the French speaking minorities in Canada. It is my belief it would not serve the national interest to try to defeat this bill because it is imperfect. I believe we must accept the principle that minority groups throughout the country should be given recognition and that their desire to have equal rights and opportunities in one country should be facilitated.
May 23, 1969

At the committee stage we must proceed to improve the bill. Some amendments have already been suggested by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), and on our side the hon. member for Cardigan (Mr. McQuaid) outlined some excellent suggestions and amendments we will propose. As we proceed others will be developed.
The bill deals mainly with French speaking minorities outside of Quebec and English speaking minorities in Quebec. The question is rightly asked, what about other minority groups in Canada, those who speak other languages and want to use them? The bill gives those groups nothing more than a casual nod in their direction, a recognition that they exist and nothing more. The government in fact has done nothing to meet the desires of these other groups to become part of Canada and yet retain their cultural and linguistic identity within the country. This is one of the main reasons there is hesitation about adopting the bill. But it does not make the bill itself and the principle any less valid, nor does it justify my voting against it, imperfect and weak thought it be. The intent is to recognize the longstanding feeling by many French Canadians that they are strangers in their own country.
The government may not be moving in the right direction with this bill nor in the proper manner, but the government members are the only ones who in the next two or three years can move at all and it is better they should move than stand still. It follows, therefore, that I must support this bill on second reading without any reservation whatever as to the principle but with considerable doubt about the details.
There have been many speeches during this debate and I have listened to almost all of them. The views put forward by hon. members have been very seriously considered and every hon. member has been forthcoming in his views. I must say, however, that I found it very depressing when the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy) on Wednesday night stood in his place and called others bigoted. I must say that he made what I thought was the most bigoted and provocative speech in this debate. I believe he committed a gross falsehood by calling others bigoted. This does nothing whatever to advance the cause of good will and better understanding in a very difficult situation when many people of good will are trying to represent their ridings, present their views and put forward the very deeply held feelings of their constituents.
Official Languages
The Confederation for Tomorrow conference of all the provincial premiers, held in Toronto in 1967, unanimously adopted the principles upon which this bill is based. A detailed statement of consensus was issued by the premiers at the conclusion of the conference. Similar views came from the federal-provincial conference of 1968. However, at a later conference called by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) it appeared, unfortunately, that the attitudes of some were hardening. I do not think there was any change in the general good will or the general understanding of the principles but rather a hardening because of the way in which the present Prime Minister was proceeding. Rather than advancing the cause of good will and better understanding in Canada, which he led many Canadians to believe he would do when elected Prime Minister, I believe that by ineptitude or carelessness he permitted the situation to deteriorate by allowing positions to harden and old attitudes to be re-established.
I believe that is a tragedy. However, inasmuch as the principle of providing services in the second language in areas of Canada where a substantial minority exists has been established, surely it would be foolish now to abdicate this principle so substantially adopted by those responsible for all the governments in Canada. There were then, as there are now, doubts and reservations about the methods of carrying out this consensus or understanding, but how else could we expect Canadians to react? We have a diverse country. People in one area may have no understanding whatever of the problems of other areas. This is inevitable in this country, and it is inevitable that Canadians will be divided on matters in respect of which they really have no contact. In spite of the difficulties we must try to straighten out, in spite of the doubts we must try to rectify, in spite of the errors made in drafting the bill which we must try to correct, there can be no doubt whatever about the principle.
[DOT] (12 noon)
As I said in the beginning, this bill does: not move very far in the civil rights field. It does not outline a bill of rights for all Canadians, either in a federal statute or embodied in the constitution. It does nothing to alleviate poverty; to bring our native Indians into the abundant life of the late 20th century, or to recognize equality of opportunity for those who speak other than English or French. It does not move against racial discrimination in the broad sense but deals

May 23, 1969
Official Languages
mainly with language matters for one group of people. Because of the diversity of our people and our customs, and because of the many different circumstances in which each minority group across this country lives, we cannot be positive that even the bill as proposed to be amended will meet the intended purpose.
This bill attempts to deal with longstanding grievances of one specific and large group of Canadians. There is no use in my standing here and saying these grievances are imaginary or that a better way can be found if -we wait a while. No doubt a better way will be found, and perhaps another government will find it. There is no use in saying that many other grievances are not covered or that many other groups have been overlooked or ignored. Another government will correct these difficulties and there are more grievances which must be dealt with soon, but we must apparently wait for that day. The government has moved in a very narrow way to solve a very narrow grievance.
Other speakers have pointed out the great problems in many areas in respect of social welfare and civil rights. I do not need to go over them again because they have been well covered. We feel that the government is avoiding these issues and that it is bringing forward other bills perhaps as an excuse for its failure to meet the real problems of poverty and regional disparity.
In spite of all these things we cannot deny that in respect of this specific problem the government is moving, perhaps poorly and weakly, to rectify it. To this extent I feel bound to support the government with the hope that the committee will rectify some of the errors in the bill with the hope that this first move will precipitate others and will encourage further useful legislation to solve some of the problems facing this country. As I said at the outset, I feel bound to support the principle of this bill, and I will vote in favour of it on second reading.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be most pleased to speak only in French on this bill, but unfortunately it is impossible for me to do so right now, because I do not know the language well enough yet. I will continue my speech in English.
tEnplish]
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Aiken) referred at the beginning of

his remarks to events that are happening in other parts of the world and the fact that the same things could happen here. I agree with him completely that if they did the results might be similar. However, this is one of the things this bill respecting the status of official languages in Canada attempts to prevent.
I crave the indulgence of the house while I make a brief survey of some Canadian historical facts as I believe they relate to this bill. In doing so I hope I will allay some of the fears, pointed out by the hon. member who preceded me, in relation to the circumstances of the so-called other ethnic groups.
More than 350 years ago there were Canadians living in North America. Their language was French. More than 230 years ago Canadians were engaged in the exploration and exploitation of the west. Their language too was French. Almost 210 years ago French troops fighting in North America lost a battle to English troops, due chiefly to the superiority of the Royal Navy, and Canadians already settled here for more than a century and a half became colonial wards of Britannia in place of Marianne.
Some years later English speaking people, again because of the fortunes of war, began to settle in Canada, chiefly to the east and to the west of the ancient Canadian heartland along the banks of the St. Lawrence. It was not for another 60 years that my own ancestors arrived here from the British Isles, and not for another 30 years did the event known as Confederation take place.
At the time of Confederation both English and French, the mother tongues of the two great immigrant peoples living in British North America at that time, were given equal status in the federal parliament, in the federal courts, and in the legislative assembly and courts of the new province of Quebec. Three years later, when Louis Riel brought Manitoba into Confederation, both French and English were given official status under section 23 of the Manitoba Act which said that either English or French may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of legislature, and that both languages shall be used in the records and journals of those houses. It also said that either language may be used by any person in any pleading or process in any court of Canada established under the British North America Act, or in any court in the province. So clearly the right of the Canadian government to deal with the matter of languages as it would apply to a new territory was there, and it certainly was not challenged at the time.
May 23, 1969



[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Incidentally, when Manitoba came into confederation the French speaking people there outnumbered the English. But this in no way suggested to anyone that both language groups should not have equal rights and privileges. Later immigrants from Ontario flooded into the country, putting the principle of bilingualism under relentless and continuous pressure. When Riel was executed years later for high treason in the Northwest Territories in 1885, the jury consisted of six men none of whom could speak or understand a word of French. I think that is relevant to our present concern about some of the aspects of this bill.
Professor George F. G. Stanley has written a very good book entitled "Louis Riel". He observes in that book that Dr. Frangois Roy, a psychiatrist, testified on Riel's behalf and was, in fact, the key defence witness and the Crown knew it. Osier's tactics-that is my great uncle-were therefore, to assume an attitude of bellicosity, to browbeat if not to confuse the witness. This passage in the book continues in the following words:
Hard pressed to answer Osier's questions in English, Roy fell back upon his own language, French, and in so doing lost much of his effectiveness as a witness, if only because of the difficulty of translating his evidence in a manner easily understood by the members of the jury.
I suggest, therefore, that history proves, from a very famous trial, that our concern over legal rights is a good one.
Be this as it may, fresh immigrants from central Europe began to arrive in the west. They, too, were allowed language privileges; at least they were allowed to use their mother tongue for instructional purposes in school. Right up until 1916 or 1915, when ten pupils in any school spoke French or any language other than English, the teaching of these pupils could be done "in French or such other language, and English upon the bilingual system". This is to be found in Manitoba Statutes, 60 Queen Victoria, C-26. Then one day in order, I presume, to make things nice and tidy and efficient for the Anglo-Saxon mind of the day, English was made the sole language of instruction in the schools of Manitoba.
In my native province things have changed somewhat for the better since then. Nowadays, under some conditions once again French may be used as a language of instruction in the school and, of course, it may still be used in the legislature and courts of record.
Official Languages
At the present time neither the Premier of Manitoba, the Leader of the Official Opposition nor the members of the New Democratic party are in opposition to the principle of this bill. But let it be noted by the so-called ethnic groups, which in western Canada now outnumber both English and French, that it is only when the French language has enjoyed full rights and privileges that then- own languages have had a chance. Incidentally, it is no accident that the present bill goes out of its way in clause 38 to ensure that "nothing in this act shall be construed as derogating from or diminishing in any way any legal or customary right or privilege acquired or enjoyed either before or after the coming into force of this act with respect to any language that is not an official language."
I suggest that history proves gradualism, advocated by several speakers in this debate, to be a mirage. Unless language rights are nailed down by law it is all too easy for a majority, made intolerant by the pressures of temporary adversity or current fears, to abrogate these language rights. That is what the so-called backlash is all about in western Canada today.
Canada is not and has never been a melting pot. It glorifies in a diversity of peoples almost as varied as the magnificent geography that we all enjoy. We on the prairies are different from some of the rest of you. We have a richer cultural diversity. We have our own unique way of looking at things, stemming from the past we have shared together and the things we have done together to make life liveable in one of the most unforgiving climates in the world.
Apart from what we are and what we have become, chiefly by our own efforts during the last 100 years, our geographical position in Canada is quite different from that which was visualized by the Fathers of Confederation so long ago. My own city of Winnipeg, for instance, is no longer the gateway to the west; rather, it is the centre of a potentially rich heartland that faces both the Pacific Ocean and the Arctic Sea. If it is a gateway to anywhere, surely it is the gateway to the north.
Because of these things, and because we incorporate joyously many cultures instead of just two, we have always rejected the two-nation theory that has been bandied about from time to time. But there is no logical reason why we in the west should hesitate to acknowledge the legitimate demands of those who insist that French should be an official

May 23, 1969
Official Languages
language. By creating a climate in which French culture can flourish, surely the principle of national diversity is ensured. As I have already pointed out, whenever we dismiss the French fact we must dismiss all the other "facts" too-the Ukranian fact, the Polish fact, the German fact, the Indian and Eskimo fact, indeed, every fact that makes our western region so culturally interesting and rich. By acknowledging the justice of the French fact, however, we infer that there is a need for a means by which the "third force" Canadians, of whom there are so many in the west, can preserve their languages and cultures wherever they are gathered in sufficient numbers so to do. Thus, wholeheartedly and with consistency, we can commend the sort of resolution adopted by the ninth Ukrainian Canadian Congress in Winnipeg on October 14, 1968.1 will read that resolution:
Now therefore be it resolved:
That pursuant to its exclusive constitutional right under section 93 of the British North America Act to legislate in the field of education, the province of Manitoba be petitioned by the Ukrainian Canadian Committee to enact legislation to protect the language and cultural rights of all persons in Manitoba of other than English or French descent by guaranteeing to all such persons, in the districts populated by the respective minorities in such of the public schools therein . .. the right to receive instruction in their respective language as a subject of study and the right to have their language used in such public schools from grade 1-
In my opinion this was a sensible suggestion for the Ukrainians of Manitoba to bring forward. It would be entirely inconsistent and untenable for them to bring forward this resolution if there were not a measure such as Bill C-120. The two things go together and are in my opinion inseparable. The country as a whole has two official languages, and a region or province is justified in encouraging regional languages.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
I am convinced that the so-called western backlash has nothing to do with the official languages bill. Those politicians from either side of the house and those public figures who pretend that it has, do themselves and their country a disservice. We need constitutional reform-yes-so that in some way we may have a more effective voice in the west than the one we enjoy at the moment. We want a greater voice in the decision-making bodies of this nation-in parliament, in the Senate, in the boardrooms of our financial and industrial concerns, and on the executives of the labour unions whose decisions affect so many of us today. We are a "becoming" nation, which is

both our glory and our cross. As westerners we want more opportunities to help decide what we become.
These are the things that worry us western Canadians, and they have nothing to do with Bill C-120 which, with amendments, is a completely innocuous and a very necessary piece of legislation. What we politicians of all parties from the west should do, after resisting any temptation to place ourselves at the head of a not so holy and utterly sterile crusade against this legislation, is to press with all our might for economic and constitutional reform that will let the west take its rightful place as an equal partner in this great Canada of ours.
Mr. Speaker, I endorse wholeheartedly the principle of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot think of a more inappropriate time for the parliament of Canada to be discussing the bill before us. Many serious problems face the people of Canada, and most of them have a great deal to do with whether or not we will remain a nation in the years ahead. None of these problems will be solved as a result of either the passage or the debate of this bill.
I represent a constituency in the Atlantic provinces. Regional economic disparity is a fact recognized by the government and by the people of this nation. The most recent unemployment figure from that area indicates that the problem continues to be serious and even chaotic. Yet the government does nothing or next to nothing except to send a new minister down to the region to talk about programs and plans that he envisages will take 15 years before having any material effect on the income and status of the people of that region. In spite of this the government says that we must debate this bill even though by its very nature and content it is questionable whether this institution should even consider it.
The government tells this institution and the people of this nation that it has the competence to produce and enact this piece of legislation even though leading jurists of this nation have expressed grave doubts as to the competence of parliament to deal with the legislation before us. While the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicates that he and his law officers are of the opinion that the bill is constitutional, an individual of no less stature than the former president of the Exchequer Court of Canada has indicated in no uncertain terms that it is his belief that parliament does
May 23, 1969

not have the competence to deal with this legislation and that it should be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada for a ruling. The three prairie premiers have also indicated their grave concern over the content of this bill and have questioned parliament's competence to deal with it. We have not heard from them since the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) indicated that certain amendments to the bill will be moved by the government. It is my hope that when the bill is referred to the committee some of the serious objections that have been made to its content will be explored in great detail.
I am opposed to the principle of compulsion so far as language rights in this country are concerned. At the same time I do not oppose a committee of this house examining in detail the content of the bill as it is placed before us because I hope they will examine in detail section 91 (1) of the B.N.A. Act and especially that aspect of it dealing with language rights. I should like to place that portion of section 91 (1) on the record which precludes parliament from dealing individually and directly with language rights in this nation. Section 91 (1) reads as follows:
The amendment from time to time of the Constitution of Canada, except as regards matters coming within the classes of subjects by this Act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces, or as regards rights or privileges by this or any other Constitutional Act granted or secured to the Legislature or the Government of a province, or to any class of persons with respect to schools-
This is the important qualification.
-or as regards the use of the English or the French language-[DOT]
If section 91 (1) is construed in a narrow sense, then it is not for us in this institution to make that decision but it is a decision to be taken by the Supreme Court of Canada. In this way language rights are placed in a strait-jacket, as was contended at the time when Prime Minister St. Laurent amended the constitution and added this section to it. If they are placed in a strait-jacket, then we do not have the competence to act on section 133 of the B.N.A. Act which outlines in detail the language rights in this nation.
In answering the Hon. J. T. Thorson on November 22,	1968, the Prime Minister
outlined his and I assume his government's attitude with regard to both sections 91 and 133. But once again the fact that the Prime Minister has taken this position does not means that it is the correct position legally. It only means that this is the attitude of the government in this regard. The only way in
Official Languages
which we can ascertain whether or not parliament can act on this bill is by referring the decision to the Supreme Court of Canada. This is the only way in which we will know whether in fact we have the right to alter certain aspects of the language rights in this nation.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
I indicated that this is the worst possible time to have a debate on a subject that is giving Canadians everywhere a great deal of concern. Today in the province of Quebec English speaking people who reside there are greatly concerned. A great many people are leaving. A great many commercial enterprises are leaving that province.

speechtext: How do you know?

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE- APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) asks me how I know. Would he not agree that Industrial Acceptance Corporation has just moved its head office from Montreal to Toronto? This is a billion dollar enterprise. If this is not an indication of what is in the minds of the people I should like to know what other evidence the minister expects to find.
When this debate was initiated some time ago we were told that all the government was endeavouring to do was to give French speaking individuals outside Quebec the same rights as English speaking individuals have in the province of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I am sure English speaking citizens in Quebec would like to know exactly what their rights are today. A bill was proposed in the Quebec legislature with an indication that those rights would be outlined. That bill has been withdrawn and there is every sign that it will never appear again.
The events at St. Leonard have caused concern to all Canadians, especially to those of ethnic origin who have great difficulty in seeing that their children receive an education in the language of their choice. These are the reasons for my saying that Canadians are concerned. The government should have taken notice of this situation by withholding action on the bill now before us until such time as there is clarification of the rights which Canadians using English as their mother tongue may enjoy in the province of Quebec.
I read the comments of the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis). He drew attention to the deep concern felt by the public servants of Canada who are unilingual.

May 23. 1969
Official Languages
They are concerned about the danger to their future employment and careers from the concept embodied in this legislation. And there is real reason for this concern because all kinds of events are taking place in this country which are most unsettling to English speaking and unilingual people in this nation. Foremost is the fact that they will become second class citizens because they do not have the second language or the capability of securing a working knowledge of the second language.
This limitation does not necessarily arise because they are not intelligent. I have never endeavoured to secure a knowledge of the French language mainly because I know from past experience that it would come very hard for me. At the same time I have tried to the best of my ability to see that my children have a working knowledge which will allow them to become bilingual in the days ahead should they desire to do so. But it is not a question of any compulsion being placed on me by anyone. I hold this view because I believe my children will be enriched by being able to speak more than one language. I have nothing against them or anyone else being able to speak many languages if that is their desire, but I do not think anyone should be compelled to secure a working knowledge of more than one language and I do not think the absence of such knowledge should in any way jeopardize his possibilities so far as employment or promotion in the government service is concerned. I do not like the idea of any more authorities being set up in Canada to make decisions as will be the case when the commissioner proposed by this bill takes up his duties.
Some of the proposed amendments cause me as much concern as does the bill itself. The proposed amendment to clause 9 reads as follows:
Every department and agency of the Government of Canada and every judicial, quasi-judicial or administrative body or Crown corporation established by or pursuant to an act of the Parliament of Canada has, in addition to but without derogating from the duty imposed upon it by subsection (1), the duty to ensure, to the extent that it is feasible for it to do so, that members of the public in locations other than those referred to in that subsection-
The reference is to bilingual districts.
-where there is a significant demand therefor by such persons, can obtain available services from and can communicate with it in both official languages.
Where would that lead us if it became law? Surely it is a provision which implies an extension of power well beyond the proposal

embodied in the bill concerning the establishment of bilingual districts.
It is my belief that we accomplish nothing by trying to impose the French language upon Canadians by compulsion. It is my belief that the schism in evidence today in this nation between the two major language groups could become an unbridgable gap if we continue the debate on Bill C-120. It is my hope that the committee, when it is established and considers this measure, will call a good deal of evidence as to the competence of the Parliament of Canada to legislate an amendment to the British North America Act, for this, in my view, is what Bill C-120 does. It is my hope that the committee will recommend that the reference which many in this country have urged should be made to the Supreme Court of Canada to determine the constitutionality of the bill in question will, in fact, be made so that we may know whether we are endeavouring to do what is right or, in the alternative, whether we are trying to do by the back door what we cannot do by the front door because it is impossible for the federal government to secure the consent of the provinces to the amendments they have in mind.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE- APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the outset of this debate, many speakers have stressed the fact that this bill will be welcomed by Canadian youth.
I wish to take part in this debate on the status of the official languages of Canada to express not so much the views of a government member, but rather the views of a 30-year-old Quebecer who, for the last twenty years, that is from the first time he left Quebec, has been asking himself many times whether he is a full-fledged citizen in this country.
Anyone who looks at the situation without prejudice should agree with me that Canadians of French language and culture do not have everywhere in Canada the same opportunities as English-speaking citizens, if they want to live, work and bring up their children in their mother tongue.
This definite situation has existed for quite some time, and it has not varied in spite of the thousands of grand patriotic speeches delivered in the past by men of authority and, very likely, of good will.
Today, this situation must change. Otherwise, I would not hesitate to predict that
May 23, 1969



Canada itself will change, and we will then see the disruption of the country.
Indeed, my generation and the one that follows do not have the patience of our parents or grandparents. We want the adoption of this bill, because we have waited a long time for it. That is the minimum, as far as we are concerned, and it is time it came about.
The vastness of our country, poor means of communication, isolation, mediocre teaching of Canadian history, a too-often unbalanced competition, have had as a result that, for years, French Canadians and English Canadians have not felt close to one another: either they knew one another not at all or very little, and badly at that, or else, more often than not, disliked one another without really knowing why.
It is easy then to understand why our parents and grandparents nursed so many grudges and prejudices.
Today, communications are much better. The young people travel a lot and the teaching of Canadian history has improved considerably. It is no longer taught, amongst other things, that the bad English encouraged the Iroquois to massacre the French, that the depraved French gave alcohol to the Indians the better to rob them.
Fortunately, my generation and the one that follows hold no grudges nor any prejudices. On the contrary, we are willing to make many concessions. We are willing above all else to pay the price so that Canadians may feel at home throughout the land.
When, in the summer of 1965, a private company made a survey across Canada on behalf of the B & B commission, Canadians under 35 who were questioned answered in a proportion of almost 100 per cent that all Canadian citizens should be able to deal with the federal government in English or in French, as they choose.
I therefore do not hesitate to say that the young people of Canada support this bill wholeheartedly. On their behalf, I urge my colleagues in this house to vote for this bill without reservations, unanimously.
Doubtless, the bill asks a generation of men steeped in prejudices to accept realities they were never ready to recognize. But, on behalf of the country they love, on behalf of the children and grand-children they cherish, I ask them to do violence to their feelings and allow a new generation of young and open minds, willing to forget their forefathers' quarrels, capable of tolerance and respect of
Official Languages
others, to build a united, prosperous and serene Canada.
It is unfortunate that some members are seeking all sorts of excuses to oppose this bill. Whether the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) was too outspoken or not, whether this bill should come before the house before rather than after the bills concerning housing and industrial incentives, that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) did not see fit to inform the house earlier of the amendments to the bill whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is in an ivory tower or not, all that, in my opinion, is quite frivolous talk in such a serious and important discussion.
May I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to tell those who have made such remarks and who would be tempted to vote against this bill on such pretences, that the young people of Canada are fed up with all their nonsense and regard them as dusty old reactionaries: the sooner they vanish from the present political scene the better.
I feel there are actually only two questions to clarify about this bill. First, can it be anticonstitutional? Second, can it cause injustices towards unilingual civil servants?
To the first question, I shall answer that, in my opinion, the bill is perfectly constitutional. I think that this bill comes under the jurisdiction of parliament. It is not in any manner detrimental to the rights and privileges granted by virtue of section 133 of the British North America Act.
On the other hand, as the Minister of Justice said in the house last Tuesday, it would not be fair to interpret the constitution so as to freeze, in a way, the use of French apart from the rights granted by section 133. The fathers of confederation conceived a bilingual Canada, a bilingual parliament, and they have drawn up a constitution in which the two languages are on the same footing.
This bill certainly does not betray the spirit of the constitution. Besides, beyond the constitution, beyond parliament, the Canadian people recognize and accept bilingualism in Canada. Gallup polls show that more than 80 per cent of Canadians recognize the principle of language equality. It would therefore be unfortunate if we were to ask the courts for a ruling on the constitutionality of the bill, because such a procedure would inevitably entail long delays.
Such a procedure would greatly antagonize-and I do not hesitate to say so-the

May 23. 1969
Official Languages
young people who want action from the leaders of this country and who are becoming increasingly impatient.
I hope the consultations the Minister of Justice had with several attorneys general have been useful and that the proposed amendments will satisfy the most fearful.
I will not enlarge upon the subject at this stage, because we will have the opportunity to look fully into the bill in the committee. It seems obvious to me however, that the Minister of Justice has done a wonderful job and that he deserves our gratitude.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
I think that the propositions suggested as a whole should be accepted by the Western provinces as well as by the province of Quebec and certain Maritime provinces. I do not think that it is necessary to have the bill in its present form with its suggested amendments referred to the Canadian courts in order to have it passed so that it may become law.
As for the second question, in my opinion, no provision of that bill justifies the fears of some unilingual officials who believe that they could not take advantage of the opportunities which they would otherwise have had.
The government has said that it is only from 1970 on that the knowledge of both official languages or the will to acquire it will be required in localities-and this is very important-where bilingualism answers a need. That is the general policy the government will follow for management and administration positions, and the same requirements will apply to promotions within the service in 1975 only.
Therefore, a person speaking English only could still be promoted in a locality where bilinguism is not required. Then, in the next few years, a unilingual person will still be able to take all means made available free of charge by the government to improve his knowledge of the second language. Therefore, if he takes the trouble, he could be promoted in a centre where bilingualism is a requirement.
Do I need to say that at present, it is essential that French Canadians know English to enter the federal public service. All that will be needed for an English-speaking civil servant to be promoted in some localities will be his will to learn French.
Mr. Speaker, some hon. members have complained that televator operators and door watchmen have been transferred because they were not bilingual. To my knowledge,

none of them has lost his job. I do not believe that they were in the government service to be necessarily in charge of a particular door or elevator. If they are working elsewhere, it is because of the circumstances, the same way as a machine operator in a plant is transferred to another job when the plant manager decides to replace his machine and to secure the services of another younger employee to operate it.
If some hon. members are too fanatical to understand that the higher interests of the country demand that those in charge of the central entrance of the parliament buildings, for instance, be bilingual, I cannot help it, but that is the prevailing situation.
In such a case, the government should take its responsibilities and transfer somewhere else the official who is not up to the new requirements. Anyway, the civil servant being transferred should consider himself lucky, as he is privileged over those who speak only French who will never be accepted in the civil service unless they learn English.
This being said, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words to those who underestimate the significance of this bill. I was surprised that even the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) did not grasp all the implications of this bill when he said on October 17 of last year, when the house was considering the draft resolution, as reported at page 1484 of Hansard, and I quote:
Within the framework of Canada's constitutional evolution and of the problems we still have to resolve, this resolution can hardly be regarded as a very significant or decisive step.
It is the Leader of the Opposition who is speaking.
As I have said, it is quite a small part of the over-all question, and from the point of view of the government it is the easiest part. All that is required is the drafting and presentation of a resolution and a bill in this house.
The Leader of the Opposition tells us that all that is required is the presentation of a bill. Yes, only that was required. Yet before that was achieved, many years went by; thousands of patriotic speeches of all kinds were delivered and it took a gallant government and, above all, a resolute and responsible Prime Minister to undertake it.
The need for an act respecting the status of official languages was one of the main conclusions of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism. The Liberal party, not the party of the Leader of the Opposition,
May 23, 1963

made it one of the planks of its election platform. The campaign of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-not that of the Leader of the Opposition-was centered round that principle. The Prime Minister laid emphasis on the equality of languages in all parts of Canada. He dealt with that subject in all areas of this country, expressing himself in those occasions in both languages. The people, especially the young ones, understood and accepted that.
Far from being an unimportant step, as suggested by the Leader of the Opposition, I believe this bill is a decisive step that will enable us to really unite Canadians by making them equal partners.
I think that the achievement of linguistic equality in Canada is at this time the most important challenge, the most urgent and most essential task, without which everything else could very well be useless.
Several of my fellow citizens at the present time preach unilinguism in Canada. An important movement advocates Quebec's independence. Obviously many have lost patience and do not want to belong to a country where you have to fight constantly to preserve your linguistic rights.
The hon. member of the opposition who spoke before me put forward the case of St. Leonard. He pointed out the enormous importance of this bill when referring to St. Leonard.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that fine speeches are not enough and that action is required. If the nice words we hear, here and there, are spoken in earnest, it would therefore be normal to put them in writing and to put in our statute books the principles recognized in the measure under consideration. Only the law can protect people's rights.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was saying, before lunch, that rights can only be protected by law, and I mean by that that it is no longer good enough to make fine speeches. If we are truly sincere and if we truly want to do something positive, it is high time that
Official Languages
we spelled out and incorporated in our statutes the principles endorsed by this bill.
I feel that to approve this bill is the best way to refute the arguments of several separatists. Then, French-speaking Canadians outside Quebec would enjoy the same rights as English-speaking Quebecers, since French Canadians would then feel more at home in every part of the country, and more especially in the national capital. It would then be possible for them to live in an English environment without giving up their cultural background.
As the Prime Minister said on October 17 last, and I quote:
-Those who argue for separation, in whatever form, are prisoners of past injustice, blind to the possibilities of the future.
Let us make the future beaming with possibilities by passing this bill, and the ghost of separation will blur away as this bill is applied progressively.
The main object of this bill is to remove cultural and linguistic inequalities in Canada. It will enable everyone to be on the same footing to develop their talents and use their energy and their knowledge for the benefit of their fellow-citizens.
I would like to recall the words uttered last Friday by the Secretary of State, when speaking to the bill, and I quote:
The bill concerns not individual bilingualism, but institutional bilingualism; that is, the use of the two languages by government services in their dealing with the public.
Members of the opposition have accused the Secretary of State of using extremist language. I wonder how his words could be construed as extremist. Further on, he said in particular that it follows from the principle stated in this bill that:
-all official documents . . . must be published in both official languages.
This legislation. . .
-provides for the establishment of federal bilingual districts in all regions inhabited by both French and English speaking citizens-
In my view, it is only normal to hope that such bilingual districts are established

*
-as long as 10 per cent or more of the population .. . use the minority official language as their mother tongue.
I fail to see anything extremist in that demand.

May 23. 1969
Official Languages
The Secretary of State also said that in the bill, and I quote:
-provision is also made for all departments and bodies of the Canadian government, all federal courts, quasi-judicial and administrative bodies and Crown Corporations to ensure that both languages are used in all their relations with the public.
I feel that it is quite normal-there is nothing extremist in that-to allow a Canadian citizen to deal with his government in his mother tongue.
Finally, the Secretary of State said:
-the bill deals with the appointment and duties of a Commissioner of official languages for Canada ... The commissioner will be responsible for ensuring that the status of both official languages is recognized in practice and that the spirit of the law and the intention of the legislator are respected in their entirety.
I feel there is nothing extremist in asking that there should be some sort of ombudsman of language matters in Canada.
In the course of our history, we have experienced rather difficult times, especially several years ago, when language and education issues arose in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and even in Ontario. I am under the impression that this legislation offers us certain guarantees through the appointment of a Commissioner of languages, who will see that the rights-I repeat-the rights of every Canadian citizen are respected. French Canadians are not asking for a privilege or a favour, but simply for the recognition of a right by this legislation.
In concluding my remarks, I would like to repeat what I said at the beginning-and I speak not only for myself, but on behalf of all young Canadians who believe in the future of the country, who are proud to be Canadians, and who want this bill to be adopted-it is the minimum and is long overdue.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE- APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE- APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the past two years the cries for national unity across Canada have been increasingly vocal, but it is about time we as Canadians recognize the fact that unity is not achieved by assimilation. It is about time we realized that the only way to achieve unity in our nation is to preserve and promote the inherent diversities of the Canadian mosaic. The French Canadian minority in Canada has a right to participate in the social and economic life of our country. It is the combination of our multi-culture expressed in the two

official languages which preserves the Canadian identity and makes it distinctive from that of the United States. It is also this combination, I believe, which could contribute much to the unity of our country.
For these reasons I should like to say at the outset that I support the principle of the bill and its referral to the committee. I believe that basically and essentially it is a civil rights bill. I think it has been long overdue and that something like this should have been implemented years ago. We must understand the minorities, protect them and most of all make sure that they become involved within our country. If we do not, then I believe we will face a danger at some future time. We have seen the conflict among many minorities in different countries. We see the strife in the United States, in Great Britain and in an exaggerated sense in the country of Nigeria. It is my belief, if we do not do something about situations such as we have in Canada, that something like this could happen here if carried to the extreme.
As I have said, I think that basically this is a piece of civil rights legislation which will guarantee the French Canadians in particular greater equity in participating in the social and economic life of our country. It is basically from this point of view as a democratic socialist that I rise to support this legislation in the hope that it will remove some of the inequities and inequalities we have in our country. I also hope that it will make Canada more accessible to both groups of Canadians. Second, this piece of legislation should help to make Canada more distinct in identity and culture from the United States. I believe it will add to the individuality of Canada as a nation and promote the Canadian conscience and attitude on national unity throughout the world.
I shall try to be brief. I want to support this bill not because I am basically either an English or French Canadian but because I am representative of the so-called third group of Canadians. I believe Canada has an advantage over the United States in that many of the cultures and languages of the third group of Canadians have been preserved because in Canada we are more tolerant in this regard as a result of our bilingual and bicultural nature. In my opinion this ethnic diversity is of value to our Canadian culture much more than is the case in the United States where it tends to go into a huge melting pot. These are some of the reasons I should like to support the principle of the bill before us today.
May 23, 1969

Some members have made a point about alienation in different parts of the country with regard to this bill. Many people have spoken of the western alienation. This is something at which I believe we should look quite realistically because there would appear to be in the west a latent feeling of alienation and mistrust of eastern Canada. I believe it has become more vocal in recent years because the farm population has faced hardships on account of the lack of grain sales, low incomes and so on. No doubt this situation will become more serious unless something is done about it. I do not believe, however, that basically it is because there is an anti-French Canadian feeling in western Canada. I think it is more a mistrust of big business and of a government that is unwilling to instigate policies of social economic change.
I believe it is unfortunate that people in this house and outside the house take the opportunity presented by this bill to exploit the anti-French feeling. As the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Howard) said, there are essentially two main groups in western Canada who vocally oppose the bill. The opposition comes first from the four western premiers and, second, from a small group of Conservatives, the same people who of course opposed the flag and the Criminal Code amendments and probably will oppose the recognition of mainland China. I do not think this is truly a reflection of the feeling of western Canadians. I believe that most people recognize that Canada is a nation with two official languages.
I do have a few concerns about the bill before us today. First of all, I believe we must be careful when implementing a bill of this nature. We must not go about forcing bilingualism on people throughout the country. If we do this I believe we will run into trouble. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) a few days ago made representations to the minister about civil service employees and employees of the Canadian National Railways, for example. I do not think we should make the lack of bilingualism a handicap to these people whether they are French or English speaking, because it can be carried to extremes. For instance, an elevator operator in a federal building in Regina or Edmonton could be demoted or not get any more promotions because he did not have a second language. These are some things we have to watch out for in the implementation of a bill of this sort.
Official Languages
Another thing that concerns me is that I do not think this bill is the be-all and end-all in regard to national unity in Canada. It is only a part of it. It is only a recipe; it is not the entire menu. It is only a web of a weaving that helps to tie the different groups in Canada together in better understanding and communication. We need complete social and economic change throughout our society.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
Taking bilingualism, for example, we are going to have to develop a bilingual program in all schools across the country both in the French speaking areas as well as the English speaking districts. To do this will require more federal aid to education in order to promote greater bilingualism in the schools. If this is done, perhaps we can have what the minister suggested in introducing the bill, a bilingual school in every major city in Canada. This is desirable provided we have federal aid to education and a large enough population to warrant it.
But, as I said before, many other things must be done in trying to achieve and preserve Canadian unity. We need many social and economic reforms to go along with the languages bill. In French Canada, French Canadians must gain control of their own destiny more than they have today. In western Canada we have to do such things as sell grain and get more income into the west; otherwise the people there too are going to feel more and more alienated. We have to recognize the poor and give them greater security with increased housing across the country. Even more important, we have to get people involved in their country and participating at all levels in life. We notice this in particular among young people who want to play some part in the decision-making process. The Indian people want the same thing; they want to have some of the say in decisions that affect their lives. I think these considerations are very important and should go hand in hand with the official languages bill. For Canadians involvement is going to have to be the most important thing.
If we are going to be an independent nation we have to start promoting more Canadia-nism at all levels of our lives. We have to do many things, for example, get more people involved in basic arts, sports and culture and more people participating toward this end. Today social development tends to cater to the elite segment of our society, while participation should be the key for all groups in society irrespective of their origin. All too

May 23. 1969
Official Languages
often funds that are spent in Canada on development of arts, sports and culture are spent on projects such as theaters in Montreal and Toronto that only cater to 5 per cent of the people of Canada. These, of course, are the top income people.
I am very sceptical about the arts centre in Ottawa. We should take care with respect to the type of programming in this centre. I notice that opening night requires a black tie and it is also very expensive. Automatically, many people are excluded from participating. I feel this is scandalous.
We see the same thing in sports. We tend to worship professionalism, the Olympic mania, if you want to call it that. We forget to get people involved in sports-in hockey, softball and other types of sports. In many cities and towns across Canada, many people cannot go to a skating rink because they cannot afford to pay the admission.
Among other things, I think we should set aside a national day for sports and arts in Canada in order to have people in all communities and age groups participating. This goes hand in hand with a bill of this sort, for it gives people a feeling for their country and its place in the world. We should set aside a day in the springtime and get people involved in a national holiday. We could take Victoria Day in order to promote Canadianism. Victoria Day does not really mean anything now to people. Something like this could do much to promote Canadian unity. Instead, Victoria day now represents a lack of imagination by the powers that be in Canada. It is a thing of the past.
I do not want to go on much longer Mr. Speaker, except to say that I support the principle of the bill and I hope it can be referred to the committee as soon as possible. However, I also want to stress again the importance of social and economic reforms and involvement of the people in their country. Otherwise the whole purpose of this bill will be defeated. Many of the speeches made on the bill will be irrelevant because Canada will not be preserved as a nation unless we do things together. With that, Mr. Speaker, once again I would like to add my support to the principle of the bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. E. Gray (Parliameniary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE- APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am neither of English nor of French origin. I was born in this country the son of European immigrants. I am proud of my origins but, at the same time, I am proud to be a Canadian.

And it is as a Canadian sharing two great heritages that I give my full support to this bill and that I urge the House of Commons and all the people in this country to support it.
It is obvious that the future unity of our country depends upon the recognition of the present situation which results from some historic facts which brought forth two linguistic communities in Canada, one English speaking and the other French speaking.
So that our country may continue to extend from one ocean to the other, this situation has to be recognized by the federal government, in order that our government may be a truly national one, made up of French speaking and English speaking people.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
Here is the purpose of this bill: to give equal status to the two official languages in the federal field. I want to point this out. The bill deals only with the equality of the two official languages. It does not grant any superior status to any ethnic group as such. In Canada, where a third of the population is made up of various ethnic origins, neither French nor English, it is the only way to act that is acceptable and suitable.
In my opinion, if the bill is really based on language and not on race, those who are members of the so-called third group must not feel wronged or concerned.
Obviously, the fact that an immigrant is neither of French nor English origin does not mean that he and his descendants will always speak mostly their mother tongue. Most such immigrants and their children speak one of our official languages and sometimes both, although they might still have some knowledge of their ethnic tongue and be proud of their cultural heritage. Most of them speak English for reasons I shall briefly mention later on.
As concerns the Anglo-Saxons who try to question the principle of the bill and allege that it ignores the third ethnic group in our country, they show a lack of information and understanding in connection with the people who are of neither French nor English extraction.
The members of the third group above all want all citizens to have equal opportunities, regardless of their racial origin. In order that the members of that third group, or at least the majority of them, may be confident of the future of this country, we must see to it that every opportunity is provided to whoever has
May 23, 1969

the required qualifications, and who is ready to work in any or both official languages, according to the needs and circumstances.
Most of the people in this third group speak English fluently, as I have said. But English is not an artificial language. It is related to a certain nation and to its culture. However, there is no question of granting special privileges to that group, because its language is used throughout the country as a result of certain historical facts.
But if it is true that the English language belongs to a certain ethnical group, namely the Anglo-Saxon and British one, it is also true that it has played a part as a national language here, which had not been played up to now by the French language. I say this because the knowledge of English has allowed immigrants and their descendants not only to find work but to participate to some extent in the community life, in most of the regions of our country where English is mainly used. This is not the case with regard to French.
French Canadians and all other Canadians consider French as the particular language of French Canadians. The reasons for that are not what they used to be. The French Canadians, who were 70,000 at first, now represent 6 million people, 5 millions of which form the greater part of the population of the province of Quebec. If French and English languages are to be equal in federal activities, then, French must be a national language in Canada as English has been for a long time. It must become the language within a community life for all those who wish to use it regardless of their ethnic origin or religious belief. French must not be considered as the private property of the French Canadian group, no more than English is considered the sole property of the British group.
I am speaking in French today to show that if the French language is to be fully recognized as an official language in Canada, at least at the federal level, it is mine as much as English.
According to the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission, as stated in the first volume of its report, equality:
-should not only be that of the two nations that have founded Confederation, but that of their respective languages and cultures, therefore that of all those who speak those languages and belong to those cultures, whatever their origin.
This is, in my opinion, the philosophy on which is based the official languages bill.
Official Languages
Its purpose is merely to assure all our citizens that they can apply to the federal government and its agencies in one of the two official languages, as they choose.
As the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) already stated, the bill deals with bilingualism related to institutions and not to individuals. The government does not intend to force English-speaking people to learn and speak French, or to force French-speaking people to learn and speak English.
And since I am referring to the third group in our country, it must be noted that clause 38 of the bill is to the effect that the legislation does not deprive any other language of its vested rights and privileges. The measure does not take anything away from the many other cultures which have added much to our life. The fact of having in Canada not one, but two languages with an official status has created a climate which increases for other cultures the possibility of their having a valid and assured place.
If the object of the bill is to suppress injustices and to solve problems, it obviously does not intend to create new injustices and new problems.
If the bill proposes the establishment of federal bilingual districts, in which some federal services will be bilingual, it will also be possible to create such districts for Englishspeaking minorities, in Quebec for instance, and for French-speaking minorities, elsewhere in the country. And if the bill proposes the appointment of a Commissioner of Official Languages, it must be pointed out that his task will be to protect the linguistic rights of both English-speaking and French-speaking Canadians at the federal level.
It is feared by some that the bill and the government's bilingual policy will adversely affect the careers of unilingual English-speaking Canadians in the federal Public Service.
Unfortunately, those who, at the present time, raise such a point, never or almost never raised it in the past-I mean quite recently-when it was hard, if not almost impossible, for a French-speaking Canadian to be hired by the public service if he had not an adequate knowledge of English and the desire to use that language in his work, and when for a French-speaking taxpayer-too often, in the past-it was difficult, if not impossible, to deal in French with the federal government to which he paid his taxes.
But in truth, the fear I was speaking of is groundless in my opinion. In that connection,

May 23, 1969
Official Languages
I think that the policy of the government is clear. Its policy, according to the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), has provided that from 1967 reasonable competence in both official languages or the desire to get it, by attending adequate training courses-at the government's expense-should be a criteria when choosing university graduates as trainees in administrative posts in areas where bilingualism meets a need. These same principles apply to both French and Englishspeaking Canadians.
This means that it is not necessary to be fluent in French to be hired, but only to show the will to learn French-at the government's expense-after having been hired. And this will only be required for certain civil service positions where bilingualism is a prerequisite.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
One must not forget that the main object of the public service is to serve the public. And in order to do this, one should have the required qualifications. And when the work to be done requires contact with the public, one of the qualifications must be to be able to communicate in the official language used or preferred by the individual citizen.
Judging from the increasing number of applications for employment in the federal public service from English universities' graduates English speaking graduates are not at all afraid of being victims of discrimination. They are obviously not afraid because they feel as able to learn French, whenever French is needed to hold certain positions, as the French speaking employees have been able to learn English for years in similar circumstances.
There are proofs that our young people recognize the soundness of the principles of this bill. Young Canadians have more faith in themselves and in their ability than some people who have doubts about the future effectiveness of the bill before us.
But one must not forget what the government said, namely that it will not apply this legislation and this policy in an unequitable way as regards present unilingual civil servants or unilingual people wishing to enter public service. Merit will remain the basic principle of public service, and that is corroborated by one of the amendments moved the other day by the Minister of Justice <Mr. Turner).

However, one must not forget that the knowledge of both official languages can obviously enable a better qualified candidate to be superior, as to merit, for holding a position, especially if it is one where he will have to be in contact with the public, using either of the two languages.
It must be pointed out that the provisions of the bill are flexible and will give the time required to adapt the structures and to train the personnel. This is also confirmed by some of the amendments proposed by the Minister of Justice.
Once the act comes into effect, it will be applied gradually as our human and financial resources will allow.
It is true that bilingualism at the federal level will entail certain expenditures. But, to my mind, these will not be too high and we will realize that the implementation of this bill will enable us not only to have a country, but to benefit from the advantages of living in a country where the official languages are of world importance. I see that as a positive advantage instead of a crushing burden.
The growth of our economy depends, to a large extent, on the increase of our exports as well as access to the most recent technological developments. As I said, French is a language of international importance. It will therefore enable us to have direct access to foreign markets and technological progress not only in English but also in French.
We also want to remain an independent country. But our powerful neighbour to the south shares this continent with us. To remain independent, we must have a truly Canadian identity and the will to keep that identity alive. The fact of having two official languages and their interplay in our country are two factors that are essential if we want to maintain our identity and, consequently, our independence.
I started my remarks by saying that I was speaking like a Canadian who was the son of Canadians who had emigrated from Europe. Europe as well as Canada have suffered from the effects of misunderstanding, of prejudice and of extremism. We should therefore get acquainted, when we are at school, with the European past and with our own.
Our future depends on greater understanding and more goodwill. We should not only do our best to understand each other but also consider good relationship between both our linguistic groups as a golden rule and an essential policy.
May 23, 1969

To sum up, in a few words, the substance of this bill on the official languages, I think it will be simply fair to try and do to others what we would expect from them if we were in their place. They can certainly trust in the future of a country built on such a principle. And it is perhaps, also, a symbol of our present and our real future that the name of our country, Canada, is spelt exactly the same in French and in English.
In order to bring about this future, we must support this bill and continue to work like men of goodwill in order to create a country, a Canada, which will be that of French-speaking and English-speaking people, regardless of their religion or of their origin. A better Canada in a better world.
