subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE- APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on this important piece of legislation I wish to say that I believe it to be a continuation of the dialogue that has been going on for some time in Canada. I also say with no hesitation that the government is rushing this dialogue, has come to a conclusion on it and in fact is forcing a decision far too soon before the people all across Canada have had ample opportunity to become really fully involved in the dialogue and to understand the full meaning and logic of the aim of the legislation which is that Canada should become a truly bilingual country. If Canada and Canadians accept this decision, then I have no hesitation whatsoever in saying that I also fully agree with it, but I want to have an equal opportunity to contribute to the dialogue on the bilingual country which we are to become. In my opinion this bill is poor legislation which is being hurried through the house in order to curtail the dialogue before the people of Canada have really understood it or have become involved to a great extent in it.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), who introduced the bill, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), who spoke on the bill, have all said that the main purpose of the legislation is to create greater unity in Canada. It is my belief that this bill might well do the very opposite. This is why I am so concerned about the curtailment of the dialogue and a conclusion being reached before everyone in all parts of Canada has become fully involved. We are told that this legislation is not being forced down anyone's throat. How
Official Languages
can legislation really be effective if the people of Canada do not understand its spirit? I believe they would have understood the spirit of the legislation if the dialogue had been allowed to continue for some time until the full meaning of bilingualism was understood across the country.
I think there is much truth in what Premier Robarts had to say at the last confederation conference in February of 1969. I should like to read this paragraph from page 227 of the report:
We do not think that the place of the two official languages in Canada can be solved simply by means of directives, regulations, legislation, charters or indeed constitutions. We think that we must take steps of this nature, of course. But we think we must also have in the country a willingness among Canadian people to act in a generous and fair manner in the question of language usage. We do not think it is only a question of legalities. It is much more than that. It is a question of heart. It is a question of conscience. It is a question of attitude, a question of thoughful attitude.
I think that Canadians all across Canada could have drawn the same conclusion eventually as Mr. Robarts has so clearly and vividly outlined in the paragraph which I read had the dialogue not been cut off.
As to the constitutional question, the Minister of Justice said it is a political and not a constitutional or legal question. The minister was very weak in his defence of that argument. I would never seek him as a lawyer to defend me after having heard how badly he defended this legislation. There is no question about the fact that this is a strictly legal and constitutional matter which should be settled by the provinces that make up confederation. Agreement should have been reached on the matter before the legislation was proceeded with. There is plenty of evidence to suggest that such agreement has not yet been reached. Yet the Minister of Justice suggests that this is a political issue which should be settled through politics.
Many hon. members who have taken part in this debate have said that this is a political issue which was settled in the last election. At the time of elections politicians are sometimes inclined to make promises which cannot be kept and are sometimes apt to use any method in order to get elected. There is no question in my mind that during the last election this issue was used as a political gambit as a result of which people throughout Canada have become confused. This issue was presented with no clarity or succinctness.
Official Languages

May 23, 1969
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
The Prime Minister suggested that he believed in one Canada. He went out west and said he would hold the line in Quebec. He went into Quebec and said, as he was justified in saying, "We must make room for you in the rest of Canada." But what was done to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) at that time? He was misrepresented all over Canada. No wonder people have such a disgust for politicians, when they cannot resist the temptation to play politics with vital issues which can affect the country for years to come.
The hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Chappell) said the other day: "I accept the principle of two founding nations." Mr. Speaker, what ridicule some members of the Liberal party heaped upon our leader when he was going across Canada trying sincerely to bring about an understanding of this issue and made similar statements! And similar things were said by other Conservatives. Now the hon. member for Peel South tells us he accepts the principle of two founding nations. I shall not belabour the point. Unfortunately, it shows that politicians are ready to play politics with the heart issues of this country and to becloud these issues throughout Canada. I am sorry this had to happen.
There is no question in my mind that the bill before us will not lead to unity. Indeed, it is more likely to produce a further distinction between Canadians. I believe the Prime Minister was clear as to the kind of Canada he wanted, and in this connection I should like to quote from Hansard page 8907. The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) quoted, in the course of his speech, what the Prime Minister said last October:
Canada had to survive as one national state. Within this state there is no room for special status and there is no room for a degree of autonomy granted to any province which is not available to any other province.
What about the bilingual districts? Do they not fall into the category of special status? They will fall into it very quickly, whether or not the Secretary of State recognizes this.
There is no doubt in my mind that this is a legal constitutional issue. Sections 91(1) and 133 of the British North America Act make this abundantly clear. After reading these two simple sections I am convinced that even if it is not a legal, constitutional question it is a moral, constitutional matter and that the government has a moral obligation to seek a full

understanding of this legislation before proceeding with it further.
The Minister of Justice had this to say as reported in Hansard on page 8837:
It is our hope that the provinces will wish as quickly as possible to take steps to achieve the goals which all governments set for themselves at the constitutional conference in 1968. Indeed, we should not forget that the Confederation for Tomorrow Conference convened in Toronto by the Prime Minister of Ontario in 1967 accepted the principle of linguistic equality within Canada for Canadians.
What was the conclusion reached by the constitutional conference of 1968? The Prime Minister spelled it out very well when he initiated the discussion which took place at the constitutional conference held in Ottawa in February of this year. He said this, as reported at page 215 of the report, setting out the final conclusions of the 1968 conference:
Recognition by this conference that as proposed by the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism and as a matter of equity French speaking Canadians outside Quebec should have the same rights as English speaking Canadians in Quebec.
But this does not necessarily mean there should be complete equality throughout the rest of Canada. This seems to me to have been a poor reference for the Minister of Justice to use.
As to the constitutional issue, it seems obvious to me that the constitution of a young and growing nation such as Canada is bound to grow too; it has to make provision for growth. If anyone doubts that statement, let him look at what has happened in the past. The growing tree principle is well established in law. This is the principle the Alberta government encountered in the late thirties in connection with money. The same has to be true with regard to people. The constitution has to grow and it has to make provision for growth, particularly in a country as young as Canada and with so much potential as Canada.
This languages bill will become part of Canadian life, but it allows for very little growth. Perhaps I am thinking in this way because I come from western Canada. I do not really believe so. My father was born in the province of Quebec and there are many relatives of mine still living in that province and enjoying a good life there. I was born in a Russian community in Saskatchewan. I saw those people come to Canada. The Canadian government encouraged them to settle in western Canada. It encouraged them to fight nature in that hard, harsh country, as many
May 23, 1969

thought it was in the twenties and thirties. I saw the energy and the effort those people devoted toward making their contribution to Canada. I saw the desire of those people to become full Canadians. The first generation was eager to attend university. They made a solid contribution to science, medicine, law and agriculture in this country and they have earned their right to participate in the national life to the full; they have earned the right to become full Canadians. This languages bill which will become part of our constitution will prevent them, in today's society, though maybe not 10 or 50 years from now, from reaching their desired goals. This is one reason I consider the present bill to be poor legislation.
Whether we like it or not, this bill will become part of the life of Canada. I accept without hesitation the principle that confederation in 1867 was the coming together of the two founding peoples, the French and the English. I accept this readily. But we must not make it difficult for other people to become full Canadians. If it is the intention of the government that Canada shall become a fully bilingual country, I would have no hesitation about getting with it. But in this case the government should have announced, as a first step, that it was prepared to contribute toward the cost of sending additional teachers to the vast area of western Canada, to Newfoundland and to every nook and cranny of this country where people have no opportunity to learn the other language. In Quebec the same course should be followed.
If it is the desire of the government to make this country fully bilingual it has a duty to give everybody an opportunity to contribute and participate fully in the life and affairs of the country. The bill before us would prevent the people of Newfoundland, for example, from making the contribution they would like to make within the next 10 or 15 years until they become proficient in the other language. It would have the same effect upon the people of Quebec who have not learned the other language. This bill will do the same thing for the people in that vast area west of the Lakehead.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
There is no question in my mind that the first step the federal government should have taken was to give everybody the opportunity to contribute. Then, the government could have introduced its language bill, instead of bringing it in now and ostracizing or putting up barriers against those people who have
Official Languages
worked hard, are eager to contribute and who want unity as badly as those in other parts of Canada. To me, Mr. Speaker, we are making a tragic mistake.
This is not a new experiment. We are going through a period of constitutional reform; there is no question of that. As reported at page 8837 of Hansard the minister said that we must bring national unity to Canada, particularly in this period of constitutional reform. However, I suggest we should be a little more careful about the results of this dialogue.
Many hon. members have said that this bill is an experiment; that Canada is launching itself upon a beautiful experiment. I think that was said by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and perhaps by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) as well. Indeed, it is always very interesting when scientists contrive to mix a formula and create a positive result. All of the ingredients in the test tube must be apportioned very carefully.
It seems to me we believe that just by placing the two national languages into the test tube we will reach our desired goal. This might be the case if all the other elements in our society were non-contributory. No experiment has ever been done so blindly, so do not be surprised, Mr. Speaker, if the desired result is not obtained. The whole purpose of a scientific experiment is to achieve a goal. In order to achieve that goal you weigh each ingredient very carefully, keeping each free from contamination by the others. Only then, perhaps, can you achieve a positive result. In the present situation it is practically impossible to keep all of the ingredients from being mixed together. Consequently, we may find that this particular experiment will not turn out very satisfactorily.
Many people have made derogatory remarks about western Canada's contribution in this regard. We have been called fossils, bigots, uneducated, and so on; I could go down the list. I wish that those who level these accusations would examine the reason that people in western Canada feel the way they do. Some 50 per cent of the people in the provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta have an ethnic origin that is other than French or English. If anybody doubts those statistics may I refer them to the first volume of the B and B commission report. About 36.6 per cent of the people in the province of British Columbia have an ethnic origin other than French or English. It is, therefore, no wonder that people in some areas of British Columbia find themselves without an

May 23, 1969
Official Languages
equal opportunity to contribute to every phase of development within our great country.
I suggest that once again in that wonderful area west of the Great Lakes the people will find themselves having to fill out forms to determine what kind of Canadians they are. This practice will once again become evident. We will find people in that particular area being referred to as hyphenated Canadians. There is no doubt in my mind that the people in western Canada today are already what they regard as the best kind of Canadians- only one kind. Whether people are born Canadians or are naturalized Canadians, their citizenship is accepted and that is all there is to it. I suggest that this bill will put us back to that difficult period of the late twenties and middle thirties so far as this particular issue is concerned. To introduce this bill at the present time is, to me, a mistake.
With regard to the bilingual districts that are going to be set up across Canada, if we educated the people and gave them an incentive to become fully bilingual then the bilingual districts would not be necessary. Canada would become a fully bilingual country, and proud we would be of that fact. On this question I think Premier Bertrand of Quebec was exactly right when he said, as reported at page 223 of the conference report:
In any event, in practice the entire province of Quebec will be a bilingual district. Conversely, however, bilingual districts in other provinces may quickly turn out to be what, in certain cases, has been referred to as "reserves" or ghettoes.
Since I am quoting the premier I might as well place another statement of his on Hansard. As reported at page 376, in referring to his position, Premier Bertrand said:
-our representatives were opposed to the very idea of bilingual districts.
Premier Bertrand does not feel particularly enthused over bilingual districts in his province. He does not feel particularly enthused over bilingual districts in other parts of Canada, or about the contribution that people of his ethnic group will make to Canadian society in those areas.
This bill will cause disunity at the community level. It will cause unrest at the community level, and this unrest will grow. Having used the word "unrest" I am reminded of the unrest that exists throughout the world today, particularly in the country of our great neighbour to the south. I am also reminded of the unrest that is creeping into our society, our universities, among some of our farmers and the underprivileged in other areas.

I am given cause to wonder at the manner in which this bill is being brought forward. I am wondering whether we really want the bill to be successful in view of the way we are carrying out this experiment. We are running headlong into the experiment without first making a sound financial contribution to the education and enlightenment of the people. If this approach were adopted the people would have a full understanding of what a great country this could become if we were all bilingual.
With regard to the agreement that was reached with Quebec at the conference in 1968, I should like to ask how English Canadian have been treated in that province during the last couple of years. We have all heard about the desire of some people in St. Leonard to have their children educated in English. We all heard about the grant to McGill university a couple of years ago and the difficulty that university experiences because it is regarded as an English university. We have all heard that the minister of culture in the province of Quebec has declared it is wrong for any person in Quebec to take English before reaching grade 9. In western Canada today we are attempting to do the same thing as far as French is concerned but we require a little more help in getting sufficient French teachers.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
The educational authorities in Alberta are trying to begin the reaching of French in Grade 1 and would do so if only they could be helped with the cost of the program. Yet a directly opposite approach is being taken by the authorities of that great province which has contributed so much to Canada. I refer to the studies undertaken in Quebec to determine ways in which French can always be maintained as the major language there. That sort of action does not suggest that both languages will enjoy equal status, in that province as this bill suggest they should.
I think there has been much misunderstanding about the conclusions reached at the conference of 1968. Certainly, the western premiers made known in the conference of 1969 that they were opposed to the principle of this bill. There is no question in my mind that the creation of bilingual districts will create ghettos. Some have said to me, "Jack, don't worry about that; western Canada will never become fully bilingual." That is precisely the point, Mr. Speaker.
If the idea behind this legislation is to prevent western Canada from becoming fully
May 23, 1969

bilingual, then I say it is sinful. Western Canada must play its full part in the Canadian political spectrum. Of course, if the commissioner to be appointed under this bill tries to force our people to become bilingual, he may well put their backs up thus defeating the purposes of the bill. I suppose that is why many people have said to me, "Fear not; if they bring bilingual districts eventually to western Canada the people in them will live in French speaking reservations or ghettos." I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is bad to condemn people to live in ghettos or reservations. It was wrong to force our Indians to live on reservations, and our Indian people say that themselves. When they live on reservations they are precluded from participating fully in our society.
Considering all these things, I say without hesitation that unless Canada in some way can become a fully bilingual country this measure will fail completely in its purposes and divide instead of unifying the country. Those living in French speaking ghettos will not be helped by this legislation.
Much fear has been expressed in certain quarters that civil servants will be affected by this measure. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), in several soothing, reassuring statements, has said that it will not affect civil servants. What poppycock is this, Mr. Speaker? Of course they will be affected. Bilingual civil servants now receive a premium of 7J per cent of other salary. The Minister of Justice said, "But you need not be individually bilingual; we are thinking of institutional bilingualism." I ask, if a bilingual public service is not the ultimate aim of the government, why is it paying a premium of 7J per cent of their salary to bilingual civil servants? We all know that the government prefers to have fully bilingual heads of departments. I think corporations in the Ottawa area also prefer bilingual personnel.
The Minister of Justice may say that the government is concerned about institutional bilingualism, but the fact remains that bilingual civil servants are paid 7J per cent extra. I am told that the bilingual preference payment is to be increased. Clearly, there is no question about the direction in which the government is heading. Under this bill senior civil servants will have to become bilingual. It is as simple as that. A reading of clauses 9, 10 and 11 will support my contention. I think clause 36 spells out certain relevant details connected with the point I am discussing. In other words, if you want promotion in the
Official Languages
federal civil service, in the armed service or in the R.C.M.P., or in any agency affiliated with these bodies, you will need to be bilingual. Clause 10(1) reads in part:
Every department and agency of the Government of Canada and every Crown Corporation established by or pursuant to an Act of the Parliament of Canada-*
That wording embraces the Canadian Wheat Board. If the Canadian Wheat Board comes within the terms of this bill you must, of necessity, include every grain elevator in western Canada because the grain elevators work in conjunction with the Wheat Board. Let's not kid ourselves; let us not try to pull the wool over anybody's eyes. Let us not play politics with this issue but let us be frank so that we may all understand what this legislation is intended to do. Surely, if a bilingual country was desired we should have made certain the other language was adequately taught across Canada. As a western Canadian and as a member here speaking for western Canada, I say that our people are complaining loudly because they are not being given a full or fair chance to participate in the decision making and policy making in this country. They complain that they do not have an adequate chance to participate in this country's administration and that the government is not aware, as it should be, of the problems of western Canada.
The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) has enunciated our oil problems. I am reasonably familiar with our grain problems and have had difficulty in convincing the government that they are as serious as they are. The people of western Canada complain that the federal government pays inadequate attention to a whole gamut of problems. They ask, how will it help us if top civil servants must be bilingual? They fear that few from western Canada will be promoted to the top ranks of any agency or department of government since few of them speak French. Many of our people have not had the opportunity to learn the other language. Only about 3 per cent of the population of Alberta is French speaking, the figure being lower for British Columbia. Less than 7 per cent of the people of Manitoba speak French, and only a nominal number in Saskatchewan speak the language. Many of our people, as I say, just have not had the chance to fully become Canadians speaking both languages, as this bill suggests they must. Can you blame our people for looking askance at the Minister of Justice even when he reassures us that civil

May 23, 1969
Official Languages
servants will be selected and promoted according to merit?
An amendment to this bill suggests that civil servants will be selected and promoted according to merit, as that term is spelled out by the Public Service Employment Act. But the Public Service Employment Act says that bilingual employees will be given preference. It is that simple. Where is the merit, then? The ability to speak both languages will weigh heavily in decisions affecting merit. The reassurance the amendment seeks to give to some is a false reassurance. We cannot, therefore, in all conscience support this bill. Why should we? We all know of the statements made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier). He is to report to parliament on the actions of the commissioner to be appointed who, under the proposed amendments, will be a very powerful individual. He will be able to direct, manipulate and send money out to various regions. The Minister of Justice suggested bilingual districts would receive additional financing to promote and maintain themselves. People living outside of bilingual districts may not receive the same contribution from the federal government to learn a language they have not previously been able to learn. I believe this is completely wrong. When talking to members of parliament from all parties they say, I must support the bill because if I do not then Canada will separate. This bill is poorly understood and I do not think it will have any success in holding Canada together.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
I have listened to and read most of the speeches regarding this bill. No one has been able to convince me there is enough strength and meaning in the bill to keep Canada united. Canadians are being asked to place a false hope in this bill. These hopes will be dashed by the waves. The Minister of Justice could logically be accused of attempting to play politics with this bill. A headline in the Windsor Star states: "Turner urges no court test. Challenge to bill 'tragic'." There is a picture of the minister speaking before microphones along with this article. The minister said, if we lose there will be separation; if we don't we will remain united.
A headline in the Toronto Telegram reads, "Turner to provinces: 'Don't kill Bi-Bi.' " I presume this statement is directed to the four western premiers, and more particularly to those who have suggested they are going to
[Mr. Horner.)
challenge the constitutionality of this measure. Let us quit playing politics. Let us continue the dialogue, be frank, above board and open with one another. All Canadians should understand and know the full implications of this bill. In one newspaper article the following appears:
The Prime Minister drew heavy applause from the 3,000 guests in the university arena when he said his government is firmly resolved to contribute to the resurgence of the French speaking minority across Canada.
Statements such as that will not promote unity. If the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is resolved to make us all bilingual he should give us all an equal opportunity to become bilingual, but he is not prepared to do that. The Prime Minister is prepared to create disunity because he wants to reassert himself.

subtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING STATUS AND USE- APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 17, 1968, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) introduced Bill C-120, which is the subject of the present debate. The provisions embodied in the bill are a declaration that English and French are the official languages of Canada for all purposes of the parliament and government of Canada, and that all federal notices shall be in both official languages. In addition, the bill seeks to ensure that all departments of the federal government shall offer their services to the public in French and English. One of the important features of the legislation is to ensure that persons appearing or giving evidence before federal judicial bodies may be heard in the official languages of English or French.
In my constituency there are comparatively few French speaking persons. Fort William, in its early days, had several hundred French speaking families of French Canadian origin. However, with the step-up of immigration and the influx from the British Isles and Continental Europe, Fort William became more cosmopolitan in character. The roots of its culture were in many lands. But for all practical purposes, English was the only language in use. Those of French speaking origin became absorbed into the fabric with the rest of the population.
It was fitting and proper that the principal recommendations of the B. and B. royal commission should be contained in the bill because, happily, they are endorsed by the leader of the official opposition, although
May 23, 1969

there has been open resistance to them by some members of his party.
In a recent issue of the Montreal Gazette the editor pointed out that many English speaking Canadians have criticized French Canadians for being withdrawn, living a life unto themselves, behind the barrier of an antiquated provincial autonomy. But if in the future the French Canadian is to be not merely a Quebecker but truly a citizen of all Canada, he will naturally wish to be as much at home anywhere in Canada as he is in Quebec now.
At a Transport Committee meeting held in 1962 one of the then members of the Social Credit group from Quebec asked the then President of the Canadian National Railways, how many held the office of vice-president in the C.N.R. The answer was 16. The president was asked how many of the 16 who hold that office were French Canadians. He reluctantly admitted there were none. No French Canadian, said the president, had been appointed because none had been found with the required qualifications. This exchange, which occurred in the railway committee room sparked a reaction which, I believe, gave birth to the separatist movement which has since made inroads in a province that gave Canada a Laurier, a St. Laurent and our present Prime Minister. It is easy to see that the purpose of this bill is to rectify a long standing grievance among French speaking Canadians.
Ever since my election to the House of Commons 11 years ago I have been a constant advocate of French and English bilingualism, as I consider it to be the very cement which binds the founding races into a united Canada. The languages bill, once translated into legislation, will be not only a unifying force but it will be a potent device, if I may call it so, which will ensure the preservation of our district Canadian identity. I am convinced that its implementation will strengthen the fabric of our nation by easing the effort of understanding each other.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Some members of the opposition have said that the government should have given priority to other business, but what other business could be more important than good will, understanding, and unity within the nation? Others have entertained fears that the passage of this bill would mean that senior positions in the public service would automatically go to French speaking applicants at the expense of English speaking civil servants.
Official Languages
The hon. member who preceded me in the debate expressed his doubt about the wisdom of this legislation which in his view would divide rather than unite. He could not be further from the truth. These unfounded fears cannot be but the product of prejudice or partisanship. I hope neither of these passions will prevail to spoil the general goodwill which, in my constituency at least, seems to be in obvious evidence since French is now being taught in all elementary public and separate schools in grades 7 and 8. Beginning with the school year in September 1969, this practice will be extended to grades 4 and 5. This augurs well for the practical implementation of the spirit of the languages bill in the very young.
The status given to French instructors in public and separate schools by the Ontario government is, in my view, the real hope for bilingualism. If this policy were adopted by the other English speaking provinces, it would go a long way toward ensuring that English speaking pupils would become bilingual. As everyone knows, the bill itself reflects the recommendation of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism that English and French be used in government services relating to the public. In other words, a citizen, when dealing with agencies of the federal government, may use either English or French.
The province of Ontario has already indicated that in areas where at least 10 per cent of the population is composed of people who speak an official language other than the one used by the majority, which in Ontario would be English, all services will be made available in both official languages. In districts such as Thunder Bay and other similar districts dual language services will not be enforced and, therefore, civil servants will not be required to speak both languages. In short, no one will be forced to speak either English or French. On the other hand, the fact is that Canada began as a nation with two basic language groups.
Now, approximately 14,500 thousand people speak the English language, 6J million people speak the French language and about 3 million Canadians of other origins speak a third language in addition to French or English. Of course, these various cultures and languages have enriched our nation beyond compare.
At this point I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister for not delaying the introduction of this bill because it relates to a

May 23, 1969
Official Languages
fundamental question which should be decided as quickly as possible. I should also like to commend the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) for his excellent presentation of the bill. A great deal of credit should go also, to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) for his fearless and unequivocal determination to stand behind the principles of the bill and for demolishing any misunderstanding existing in the English speaking provinces that the bill is designed to force the average citizen to speak French.
This bill was never designed to achieve compulsory bilingualism but rather to provide equality of opportunity to use either language in communicating with the federal government. In an article in the Montreal Gazette of May 3, 1969 the Minister of Justice is reported to have said this:
Our policy as set forth by former Prime Minister Pearson in 1964 is that no one should be penalized for not having acquired the second language if he has not been afforded an opportunity to learn it. The key to this policy is that an opportunity will be given to people seeking advancement to acquire a working knowledge of the other language.
It is not necessary that a candidate be already bilingual to obtain a position within the public service in an administrative trainee capacity, which is the general category for university graduates. However, this policy makes it mandatory that any candidate indicate his willingness to learn the other language at public expense. Such a policy takes into account the fact that in certain parts of this country, the opportunities to learn the other language are very limited.
On the other hand, one could raise the point as to whether such a policy will deter English speaking Canadians from joining the public service.
As an answer to that question, I would like to quote the following figures. Since 1965-66, which is the year when this policy was made public and implemented within the public service, the number of English speaking applicants for administrative trainee positions has gone from 1,925 to 3,515 in 1967-68. Furthermore, the number of anglophone applicants for foreign service positions has gone from 697 in 1965-66 to 1,861 in 1967-68, for an increase of approximately 160 per cent over the 1965-66 figure.
This latter example becomes even more significant if one considers the fact that of all the federal departments, External Affairs is perhaps the one where the bilingualism policy has been pursued the most actively.
The public service has been a factor of national unity in the past, perhaps the greatest, because of the national character of its composition. The figures quoted show that so far our policy on bilingualism has not deterred English speaking university graduates, to say the least!
The languages bill, then, is at the core of our guarantee of the equal rights and privileges of our two founding communities.

That sums up the purpose of this bill which, as pointed out by the Secretary of State in his presentation, is to give equality, by legislation, to the two official languages of our country, in so far as the matter comes under the jurisdiction of the federal government. There is a definition given by the Secretary of State which I should like to quote:
Indeed this bill is a gesture of faith in the future of Canada, a hope and a pledge for most Canadians, who wish to fix their sights and determine their common objectives well beyond the differences that are threatening to divide us today.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I think this quotation should be inscribed in every school in Canada so that the school population may draw inspiration from it. I have heard people ask; why do we need a languages bill? We have been able to do rather well without one for 100 years; why bring this up now? The same was said in respect of the flag bill during the debate in 1964. Individuals said the old flag had served us well. Dire predictions were made that the new flag would divide the country. Happily the results were the very opposite, and I am confident that this bill will do equally as much for unity and the development of a national consciousness.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments at this second reading stage of the official languages bill introduced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) together with the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier).
Mr. Speaker, obviously we cannot be against this bill for the simple reason that pondering over every clause, one by one, as well as over the various amendments proposed by the government, we realize it is what one could call a positive bill in the sense that it acknowledges a factual situation and aims at removing some injustices and preventing others that, unfortunately, have occurred in the past. This bill aims at strengthening the ties of national unity.
In fact, we could summarize the bill under four main headings. First: acknowledgement of French and English as the two official languages of Canada, which is really nothing new and which was already acknowledged in 1848, then in 1867 and embodied in statutes; unfortunately, this was never recognized or respected.
Secondly, as far as judicial bodies, Crown Corporations, parliament and the government
May 23, 1969

are concerned, the bill is aimed at recognizing both official languages in all cases where the general public has a right to use them or where services are obtainable.
Thirdly, the bill aims at establishing certain bilingual districts, under given conditions.
Finally the bill would aim at establishing a so-called linguistic ombudsman post in order to preserve the rights of the people and to see to the enforcement of the act on official languages.
In brief, Mr. Speaker, the bill on official languages is essentially and solely the official recognition of the two languages and their use in certain areas in Canada.
The bill is but a first step towards a bicultural and bilingual country, pursuant to the agreement reached during the recent federal-provincial conferences on the Canadian constitution.
As a matter of fact, at the conference held in February 1968, the right honourable L. B. Pearson, the former Prime Minister, said- and in that, he was supported by the various provincial premiers-that an agreement had been reached in principle. That agreement provided for what the leader of the Rallie-ment creditiste (Mr. Caouette) had already been repeating over and over since 1962-it took six years to get it across-and I quote:
Recognition by the conference, as proposed by the Royal Commission, on Bilingualism and Bicul-turalism, that French-speaking Canadians outside Quebec should have the same rights as Englishspeaking Canadians in Quebec, in all fairness.
Such is the essential principle upon which the philosophy of the present bill is based. And that principle cannot be said to be false. On the contrary, we must commend the government for taking a positive step, out of that principle, with the agreement of the provinces in order to protect the rights and the interests of minorities, while protecting those of the majority.
This is a fundamental question. After all, it is nothing new. However, this is not where the problem lies. Those who want a bilingual and bicultural Canada and who want to keep Quebec within confederation are willing to acknowledge as a fact that there are two main cultures in Canada, although there are others, of course, that two languages are used by two majority groups and that consequently, we must fulfil certain obligations, recognize certain rights and a certain language equality and finally establish some areas where both official languages will be used. So, this factual situation has always existed but 29180-571J
Official Languages
was not always acknowledged, and this bill is intended specifically to acknowledge that situation.
The official languages bill may give rise to at least three basically different attitudes.
First, there are English-speaking Canadians, for whom Canada is an English-speaking country, and French Canadians, colonized water carriers.
English-speaking Canadians will not acknowledge as a fact the use and respect of the other official language, no matter what is said or done in parliament. Such an attitude, in my view, contributes to divide our country, and this is truly unfortunate in 1969.
There is another attitude, just as backward to say the least, and it is that of French Canadians who consider Quebec as their country and for whom all our ills must be ascribed to-pardon me the expression-those damned English. In my opinion, such an attitude is just as backward and negative. It can only contribute to divide Canada, build a sham China wall and aggravate economic and monetary problems in Quebec.
There is a third attitude, which I endorse, and it may be defined as follows: To every Canadian, be he French-speaking or Englishspeaking, Canada is a country which must be built on concepts of respect, equality and comprehension, equal sharing, cultural respect, economic respect and responsibility.
This language bill is not an innovation, but rather a protection. It represents an official recognition of both languages and their use in certain parts of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we have known many injustices in the past. For example, in 1864, French was abolished in the schools of Nova Scotia.
In 1871, French was abolished in the schools of New Brunswick.
In 1890, the French language was abolished as official language in Manitoba.
In 1892, French was abolished as the language of the administration in North-West Keewatin.
In 1915, for all practical purposes, the French language was abolished in the schools of the province of Ontario. And so on.
And yet, we were beyond doubt a people- Canada-with two great languages and two great cultures.
The honourable Maurice Sauve, then Minister of Forestry and Rural Development, speaking before the Richelieu club on October 19, 1967, about a dynamic nationalism, which

May 23, 1969
Official Languages
I support, and which I found quite interesting at that time, said:
-the fundamental problem facing Canada cannot be solved solely through constitutional reform since it is actually a problem dealing with the relations between English and French Canada.
He said also:
But what seems more fundamental to me is to determine whether English Canada will finally agree to share with us the power it has in the fields of business, finance, industry, politics, in the public service, and in social and cultural life.
Then he was more explicit:
As French Canadians, what matters most is to know whether English Canadians will agree to yield to us part of the ground they occupy almost exclusively in every area of Canadian life.
Mr. Speaker, such nationalism incites us to collective and individual fulfilment. We have definitely passed the survival period. We want to explode on the world, to take part fully in our society. And this desire for participation is irreversible. We want to live a positive, open nationalism, sensitive to the influence of the outside world, determined to achieve freedom and security for every Canadian. We want an economic nationalism which will give back Canada to Canadians. That is what concerns us in practice.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
But to achieve this, Mr. Speaker, one must feel at home in Canada. A great many Canadians no longer feel at home in Canada. This is a regrettable thing to discover, but true to fact. For instance, French Canadians do not feel at home in Ottawa, the Federal capital. It is sad to have to say so today, when discussing this bill on languages. Especially in the public service-French Canadians are not at home and have never been. I shall prove it beyond all doubt, if I have time.
Bilingualism is the price to pay to have a Canada at peace with itself. If Canadians are not ready to pay that price, at all levels of administration and management, if they are not ready to respect one another, to have equal rights and duties, that is because, fundamentally, they really do not want to have a Canada.
There is no alternative. The bill on languages meets with the wishes and needs of all Canadians and reflects the image of the Canada we want to have. This bill is a first step, but we must not delude ourselves.
What is really happening? What do we find, Mr. Speaker? French Canadians who leave Quebec to settle and work in another 
province automatically lose the rights and privileges they enjoyed in their native province. The same thing does not occur when English Canadians come to live in Quebec. In Quebec minorities are respected.
The other provinces should respect minorities just as fairly, otherwise national unity is all rot, and this bill nothing but a political day dream and a great exercise for intellectuals.
Therefore, let us shake hands instead of tightening our belts. Let us understand one another and live a real dialogue, not one of the deaf, as has been the case since the beginning of Confederation.
In principle,, if not in fact, French Canadians could not be heard in French in civil courts and even in criminal courts, although these come under the federal jurisdiction and should have been bilingual long ago.
The official languages bill is intended to correct the two unfortunate situations I have just described, and so much the better, Mr. Speaker.
It took a long time for the federal government to understand the problem and then to act. Meantime, many injustices and many disappointments occurred, but today the official languages bill deals with those absolutely unbearable situations and injustices and tries to remedy them. That is an excellent thing. However, let us hope now that it does not come too late.
In his own country, the French-speaking Canadian who leaves Quebec for another province is like an exile, an outcast, though he has no immigration or customs formalities with which to comply. In practice, he feels like a stranger everywhere in Canada. There again the languages bill solves part of the problem.
But we realize all the importance-and the question boils down to that-of the unlimited and deeply human understanding that will be needed to apply such a bill, otherwise it will fail completely and there will be nothing left to hope for.
But let us talk about bilingualism instead. It is more complex than the brief definition given in the dictionary, that is the coexistence of two languages in an individual or in a country.
It is obvious that the languages bill is not a bill on bilingualism, but solely a legislation aimed at having both languages recognized.
We must immediately lay the foundations of a bilingual country and that is why we must know where this policy will lead us.
May 23, 1969

It is obvious that the phenomenon of bilingualism is not necessarily of the same nature or import whether individuals or nations are involved.
One can be bilingual by personal choice, due to intellectual, material advantages, etc. but it definitely remains that bilingualism is a wealth for a country while unilingualism in Canada is an idea which can no longer be considered from the English as well as from the French point of view.
The unilingualism of a far too great number of Canadians and officials has given rise to anomalies and injustices even in Quebec. It has given rise to two great solitudes. Without doubt, one of those solitudes, the French one, was able, in this manner to ensure its survival, and even its self-achievement as an ethnic group.
But as nothing urges the other solitude, the English one, if not its own interest, to speak French, most English Canadians usually learn French only to the extent that it helps them to communicate with inferiors. For instance, it is the unfortunate situation that prevails in the public service.
Mr. Speaker, the only persons that are bilingual in the public service, are clerks and ordinary employees whose mother tongue is French. Those who speak English or other foreign languages have high managerial or administrative positions and are not bilingual. They do not deal with the public.
That is the main problem, the weakness of the official languages bill, Mr. Speaker: it will oblige all public servants and employees who deal with the public to be bilingual. Nothing indicates that something will change. The bill will not affect the administrative and the managerial levels of departments and Crown agencies, in order to give French Canadiens the positions they are entitled to. That is a grave danger of which the official languages bill does not make any mention at all.
At the administrative and managerial levels of the public service, the working language is English and French-Canadian employees can only reach such levels if they are bilingual.
Unilingual English-speaking employees, for their part, may easily, and often through favouritism, obtain managerial and administrative positions where salaries exceed $17,000 annually. They are therefore among the better-paid and their chances for quick promotion are very good.
This is the truth. And this is what I learned from the numerous questions I have put on

the order paper-close to 80-since the beginning of this session; and the replies can only be official since they were supplied by the government itself.
Two vast solitudes, two great official languages which are ignored by the high officials of the civil service!

Mr. Speaker, on May 9 I addressed a question to the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) asking him whether his department was giving consideration to implementing in some of our correctional institutions new techniques in dealing with prisoners, which have been developed and which are being implemented by a group located in the department of psychiatry at McGill. It is an interesting but sad fact that the program is being implemented not in a Canadian correctional institution but in the Clinton institution in New York State.
The problem of how to deal with people who break the law, who are convicted and sentenced to correctional institutions, is one which has concerned the people of Canada for a long time now. There have been a number of royal commissions, parliamentary committees and special committees which have looked at the question. There has been the Archambault commission and the Fauteux royal commission which is now dealing with the problem of corrections. Parliamentary committees have looked at the problem of Canadian corrective institutions and their inmates and have agreed that our correctional institutions have been dealing with the problem too much in terms of incarceration and punishment, in terms of keeping people who have been convicted locked up with little or no programs of work or rehabilitation. There has been unanimous agreement that if we are to change the trend, if we are to rehabilitate prisoners instead of simply punishing them, we have to find new methods of rehabilitation. Among these new methods is one calling for the increased use of psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, teachers and a whole team of ancillary staff.
When the public have asked why these modern methods are not used more we have been told that it is extremely difficult to put
May 23, 1969

this kind of program into effect because Canada is very short of the skilled and trained personnel which is required. One merely needs to look at the reports of the Solicitor General on correctional institutions to see that there are only a very few psychiatrists, psychologists and social service people on the staff. I know I am not far wrong when I say that there are only one or two full time psychiatrists and very few part time psychiatrists working for the department. So, I was shocked and chagrined to find that a team from McGill University has been working since 1966 at the Dannemora clinic at the Clinton Institution in New York State some 80 or 90 miles from Montreal. Who are these people? They are people who have been working at the department of forensic psychiatry at McGill. I am certain they would be able and happy to work in Canadian institutions, such as St. Vincent de Paul and other institutions around Montreal, if they were given the opportunity and the physical facilities as well as the feeling that they were wanted and needed.
I have with me some of the material which was prepared by the New York authorities indicating how happy they are to have an opportunity to use a trained and skilled team which we, ourselves, ought to be using. Let me just quote very briefly from some of the statements which they made about the program:
On June 21, 1966 Governor Rockefeller signed into law a bill permitting the Department of Correction to establish a psychiatric and diagnostic clinic at Dannemora as part of Clinton State Prison-
-the purpose of the clinic is to provide "intensive physical, mental and sociological diagnostic and treatment services", including "pre-parole diagnostic evaluation-and scientific study of the social and mental aspects of the causes of crime". -the clinic can become a laboratory for new treatment methods that might be used in all correctional institutions. It can also provide new and better methods of training personnel and thus become a centre for advanced training or a model for training in other institutions.
They go on to say:
An important feature of the new clinic is that it is to be run in co-operation with McGill University, located in nearby Montreal. McGill will prepare the plan for an "ideal" treatment centre, participate with the State and with other universities in furnishing the treatment, design the research project, and have general responsibility for the research. McGill's participation is to be under the direction of Bruno M. Cormier, M.D., director of the McGill Clinic of Forensic Psychiatry.
This is great for New York State, but in the light of our shortage of skilled and

They go on to say:
The initial McGill group will consist of one psychiatrist, three psychologists, two social workers and one group worker. (These services will, of course, be on a part time basis).
Why were these people not encouraged to work in our institutions which are so woefully lacking in staff?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the hon. member for raising this important question but I must confess that I find he is considerably misinformed. The gentleman at McGill University to whom he refers is a part time employee of the Canadian penitentiary service. He put forward this experimental scheme which is being tried at Clinton in New York State. This is, of course, an interesting and, I believe, very important experimental program. But I should add that we have a similar program running in Canada, though the hon. member chose not to speak about it. It is being carried out at the Springhill institution. It is true it is being done on a somewhat different basis because there are two views as to how the program of therapeutic communities should be administered-whether they should come exclusively under the control of the psychiatrists or whether control should involve the other forensic sciences on an equal footing. Subject to this change, we are doing the kind of work of which the hon. member has spoken in the Springhill institution.
The gentleman the hon. member speaks about has written to the department and has requested that one of these programs should be started in one of the institutions in Quebec province. This matter is receiving attention but no decision has been taken as to whether another will be started within the penitentiary service. If an affirmative decision is reached, I am not prepared to say it would be established in one of the Montreal institutions. We might start a scheme in one of the other institutions across the country because the penitentiary service is a nationwide service, and it is not necessarily valid to say that an experimental program such as this must be carried out in a particular province to suit the consultant who wishes to administer it. These things have to be evaluated carefully.
